output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Meenakshi Raman is seventy-six, a small woman with deeply lined hands from a life of scrubbing floors and wringing clothes. She wears faded cotton saris and ties her grey hair in a tight bun. She rises before dawn and walks the forest paths of the Palani hills, carrying a plastic file folder containing paper sheets printed by the university team. She writes her observations in Tamil in a neat cursive she taught herself at forty-two, after her youngest child started school and she was too ashamed to ask her daughters to read to her. She records local plant names periya maruthu, seeraagam, nochi, the parts used, the preparation methods, and dosages for fevers. She has used these remedies herself, as did her mother and the healers she now walks beside. When young researchers from Chennai write down Latin names, she stops them and asks, 'Who told you this?' They point to a book, and she shakes her head, insisting that the healer's name be on the paper, not merely hers. She believes knowledge comes from a person, not a book, and that Tamil names are not inferior to Latin ones. She requires permission before recording any name. She has twice halted documentation to ask who taught a remedy and has waited through light rain to ensure a healer's name was included. Her own name appears on consent forms only as a witness. She gives half her stipend—six thousand rupees a month—to a fifteen-year-old girl named Divya in her village, paying school fees from her own pocket without telling the researchers. She raised four married children and knows a girl's education is the only thing no one can take. She feels guilt about loving this new work, as if playing at something while her daughters still cook and clean. She is not loudly religious, but she touches the forest floor before leaving, whispering thanks to the plants and grandmothers. She is idealistic and principled, sometimes annoying co-workers by not skipping a single healer, never writing a name without permission, and refusing to assume a Latin name is better. She is old but starting out, and she tells herself she is a student again and walks faster.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

The sky turned grey over the Palani hills, and the university researchers were packing their clipboards and sample bags, muttering about rain that was minutes away. A young researcher held up a fresh specimen Meenakshi recognized as periya maruthu, but he was already writing the Latin name from his book on the label. He said, 'We have to move now, we can confirm it later,' and waited, marker poised, expecting her quick nod. Meenakshi stood in the wet leaves, knowing that if she did not speak up now, the name would be recorded without the healer who taught her the remedy.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Her sandals are damp from walking on wet leaves, and her file folder feels heavy under her arm. She has been on her feet since before dawn, but her hands are still steady from years of work. The forest has gone quiet with the approaching storm, yet she is familiar and at ease in this space. Seeing periya maruthu brings back the morning Kaveri showed her how to strip the bark and steep it for fever. The researcher's marker recalls a past incident when a name was written without a healer's consent and she had to have it struck out. The gathering grey clouds remind her of another drenching walk when she carried a specimen home to protect it.
